title: p-Smooth Numbers: All Prime Factors ≤ p
content: Defines a number as p-smooth if it is positive and every prime divisor is at most p. The condition `∀ q : ℕ, q.Prime → q ∣ n → q ≤ p` is stronger than specifying the set of primes: it quantifies universally over all prime divisors, which makes closure proofs immediate (smooth_mul checks each factor independently). The positivity condition `n > 0` rules out 0, which technically divides nothing but would otherwise admit vacuously. Four closure theorems follow: one_smooth (1 is p-smooth for any p), prime_smooth (q ≤ p prime ⟹ q is p-smooth), smooth_mul (products of p-smooth numbers are p-smooth), and not_smooth_of_large_prime (exhibits non-smoothness from a large prime factor).
mathContext: $n$ is $p$-smooth $\iff n > 0 \land \forall q \text{ prime},\, q \mid n \Rightarrow q \leq p$. The 3-smooth numbers are $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 18, \ldots\}$ (products of primes $\leq 3$). The 5-smooth numbers add $5, 10, 15, 20, 25, \ldots$, and so on.

title: foldPrimeBound: Prime Enumeration via Nat.nth
content: Uses `Nat.nth Nat.Prime k` to select the k-th prime (0-indexed: k=1 gives the 2nd prime = 3, k=2 gives 5, k=3 gives 7, k=4 gives 11). `Nat.nth P` enumerates elements of a decidable predicate P in order; here P = Nat.Prime. The `noncomputable` flag is required because nth uses classical choice. Four concrete bound theorems follow from Mathlib: fold_1_bound : foldPrimeBound 1 = 3, fold_2_bound : foldPrimeBound 2 = 5, fold_3_bound : foldPrimeBound 3 = 7, fold_4_bound : foldPrimeBound 4 = 11. These concrete equalities enable the fold level classification theorems via `rw [fold_k_bound]`.
mathContext: The prime sequence: $p_0 = 2, p_1 = 3, p_2 = 5, p_3 = 7, p_4 = 11, \ldots$ (0-indexed). So $\text{foldPrimeBound}(k) = p_k$, and the $k$-fold prime bound for fold level $k$ is $p_k$ (the $(k+1)$-th prime in 1-indexed notation). This gives: $k=1 \to 3$, $k=2 \to 5$, $k=3 \to 7$, $k=4 \to 11$.

title: IsKFoldConstructible: The Central Conjecture Encoded as a Definition
content: A degree d is k-fold origami constructible iff (1) k ≥ 1 (at least one fold) and (2) d is foldPrimeBound(k)-smooth. The k ≥ 1 condition is needed because fold_0_bound would be 2 (the 0-th prime), making 0-fold origami 2-smooth, which is not physically meaningful. The definition encodes the Alperin-Lang conjecture for all k: for k=1, recovers Alperin-Lang's 3-smooth result; for k=2, recovers 5-smooth; for k≥3, encodes the open conjecture. All 24+ theorems are proved from this definition — no axioms needed since the definition itself encodes the conjecture.
mathContext: $\text{IsKFoldConstructible}(d, k) \iff k \geq 1 \land \text{IsSmooth}(p_k, d)$ where $p_k = \text{foldPrimeBound}(k)$. For $k=1$: 3-smooth (Alperin-Lang proved). For $k=2$: 5-smooth (Alperin-Lang proved). For $k \geq 3$: $p_k$-smooth (conjectured). The badge `original` and 0 axioms reflect that this is internally consistent under the definition, not that the conjecture is proved.

title: Degree Classification: Prime Witnesses Separate Each Fold Level
content: Classifies individual primes at each fold level. Pattern for positive theorems (degree_p_kfold): use refine with fold_k_bound rewrite, then bound q using Nat.le_of_dvd (since q ∣ p_k and p_k is prime, q = p_k or q = 1, so q ≤ p_k). Pattern for negative theorems (degree_p_not_kfold): intro the constructibility hypothesis, specialize to the prime itself (hsm p_k (by decide) (dvd_refl p_k)), apply fold_{k-1}_bound to get p_{k-1}, and derive contradiction since p_k > p_{k-1}. The strict hierarchy witnesses bundle these into conjunction proofs.
mathContext: The separating witnesses by fold level: $5 \in \text{2-fold} \setminus \text{1-fold}$ (since $5 \leq 5 = p_2$ but $5 > 3 = p_1$); $7 \in \text{3-fold} \setminus \text{2-fold}$; $11 \in \text{4-fold} \setminus \text{3-fold}$. In general, $p_{k+1}$ is the separating witness between $k$-fold and $(k+1)$-fold constructibility.

title: Monotonicity via nth_strictMono: More Folds = More Constructible
content: Proves that k-fold constructible implies (k+1)-fold constructible. The key step: if q ≤ foldPrimeBound(k), then q ≤ foldPrimeBound(k+1), which follows from `Nat.nth_strictMono Nat.infinite_setOf_prime` — the enumeration of an infinite set is strictly increasing, so the (k+1)-th prime strictly exceeds the k-th prime. The infinite set condition `Nat.infinite_setOf_prime` is Euclid's theorem in Mathlib. The abstract proof works for all k at once, no case analysis needed.
mathContext: $p_k < p_{k+1}$ (strict monotonicity of the prime sequence, from $\text{Nat.nth\_strictMono}$ on the infinite set of primes). This gives IsSmooth$(p_k, d) \Rightarrow$ IsSmooth$(p_{k+1}, d)$. Chain: $q \leq p_k < p_{k+1} \Rightarrow q \leq p_{k+1}$.

title: Algebraic Completeness: Every Degree is Eventually k-Fold Constructible
content: Proves ∀ d > 0, ∃ k ≥ 1, IsKFoldConstructible d k by taking k = d. The key bound is `Nat.add_two_le_nth_prime d`: the d-th prime is at least d+2, so foldPrimeBound(d) = p_d ≥ d+2 > d. Since all prime factors of d are ≤ d (as q ∣ d implies q ≤ d), every prime factor falls below the prime bound p_d, making d a p_d-smooth number, hence d-fold constructible. This shows the hierarchy 'covers' all of algebra: no finite degree remains unconstructible forever.
mathContext: For any $d > 0$: all prime factors of $d$ satisfy $q \leq d$ (since $q \mid d \Rightarrow q \leq d$). And $p_d = \text{foldPrimeBound}(d) \geq d + 2 > d$ (from `Nat.add\_two\_le\_nth\_prime`). So all prime factors of $d$ are $\leq d < p_d$, making $d$ a $p_d$-smooth number, i.e., $d$-fold constructible.
